[Interview, 2005-09-05, News & Notes]
HOST: So we want to spend some time on the legacy of Justice Rehnquist, but first, let's ask the big question: Why has Judge Roberts, who until today was just a nominee for an associate justice, been so swiftly moved to the front of the line for chief justice?
GUEST: Well, I think it makes sense from the administration's point of view. They wanted to have somebody in place by the first Monday in October, when the court begins its new term. And they don't want the court coming into session without new leadership that they have chosen. If they did not replace Chief Justice Rehnquist, then Justice Stevens would be the acting chief justice. I don't think that's something they want, and they don't want the vacancy, period. In terms of Justice Roberts' re-nomination for chief justice, it's not really a surprise. I think that there were three options. One was to elevate one of the current sitting associate justices. The other was to nominate somebody fresh to be chief. But John Roberts is a known quantity, he's been vetted, and they have a lot of confidence in his intellectual ability, and he's going to be on the court for 30 years, if he's confirmed, as chief now. So for them, it's a move that I think has a lot of logic to it.

HOST: Let's talk a little bit about the special role of the chief justice. What, in fact is the--obviously all of the Supreme Court justices are incredibly powerful in shaping legal policy, but what does the chief justice do?

HOST: Charles, let me just ask you--I don't want to go too deep into talking about Judge Roberts before we get to Rehnquist, but you say that he, as a chief justice, will swing the court further right. What makes you believe that?

[Interview, 2006-04-18, News & Notes]
HOST: GUEST, with about 30 seconds to go, as Barbara suggests, we want to make sure that people understand that this is just the beginning.
GUEST: Well, that's right, and the primary's on Saturday. On May 20th, the general election will be held, and people, who are properly registered to vote can vote in both of those, and should vote in both of those.

[Interview, 2007-06-28, News & Notes]
HOST: I asked him if he thought this ruling was the last nail in the coffin of programs that take race and America's legal racial - America's legacy of racial discrimination into account.
GUEST: No. That was a fear that many of us shared. And today's opinion, certainly, are deeply troubling and in some respects, they lost because the two school districts that were at issue, Seattle and Louisville had their plan struck down and there are five votes that seemed to see these kinds of plans as unconstitutional. On the other hand, rather than a 5-4 split, this is more of a 4-4-1 split. It's reminiscent of the Supreme Court's decision en banc with Justice Powell's opinion bridged two camps. Justice Kennedy clearly rejects the proposition that Chief Justice Roberts and three other justices would have held that race can never be considered in assignment of public school students and that the school districts could do nothing to try to desegregate or integrate or to maintain or achieve diversity. He doesn't buy that. He thinks that there's still a compelling state interest in having racial integration in public schools and doing something about de facto segregation, as it's called, that exist. But the window is still left open. But, you know, it's still a troubling set of opinions.

HOST: To follow that point, Chief Justice Roberts wrote in his majority opinion that, quote, "The way to stop discrimination is to stop discriminating." How practical is that?
GUEST: The problem with that supposition is that it holds that trying to desegregate or integrate public schools - trying to include people is racial discrimination that is tantamount to the discrimination that black folks and other people of color suffered under the regime of white supremacy and that's simply a false assumption. If Chief Justice Roberts and those who agree with him have their way, we would be preempted from doing anything about continued racial inequality unless we could prove that the specific actor engaged in intentional racial discrimination in a very clumsy way that's clearly not enough. Look, one of the most powerful moments that I've seen in the Supreme Court occurred today and that was the dissent read from the bench of Justice Breyer, a lengthy, powerful dissent that I think anyone who's concerned about racial justice and the Supreme Court should read. But he says, before he put this is the context of our continuing struggle to overcome both our history and continuing racial inequality for one reason or another, there are four justices of the court who simply don't see that.

HOST: GUEST, your 25 years with the Legal Defense Fund career is coming to an end in February with your resignation. Rulings like this, do they discourage you, particularly, coming at the time that they do with regard to your own personal career?
GUEST: Well, first of all, while I am going to leave the Legal Defense Fund in 2008, I will never step away from the issues that I have devoted my life to and that I care about. And I refused to be discouraged. In fact, what happens is that they get my blood flowing. It convinces me that we have to redouble our efforts. We have to continue to fight, and there are moments when I may be tempted sometimes to be discouraged but I know that when that happens, we might as well lay down that the other side wins. So I've learned that hope is not serendipitous. It's a choice. And we have to chose hope and then work to make that hope reality.

h6_poor_b1000.block:
[Interview, 2005-09-05, News & Notes]
HOST: Gentlemen, thank you so much and welcome.

HOST: Thank you.
GUEST: Thank you. Good to be with you.

HOST: Let me ask you, Charles, about minority clerks. Judge Rehnquist never hired a single African-American among the 82 clerks that he had; 81 of those 82 were white, and he said, you know, `Wait for the demographics to change. There's no need for a wider net. The system is working just fine.' In your role as a Harvard law professor, do you find that acceptable? Do you find it acceptable that this pathway to the inner workings of the justice system is--has essentially been for many of the justices...

HOST: Let me ask you about whether or not the Bush administration is going to feel pressure to nominate a woman or a person of color or both for Sandra Day O'Connor's seat. Sandra Day O'Connor herself expressed some dismay that a woman was not nominated. Now that Judge Roberts is being nominated for the supreme Supreme seat, if you'd put it that way, is the Bush administration going to feel pressure to take a second look at the diversity of the court?

HOST: GUEST, what do you think the chances are for more diversity on the court?
GUEST: Well, I think that there will be some pressure in the minds of some to appoint a Latino or a woman, a Latina, or something like that, but I agree with Charles. I don't think that the president is going to feel a lot of that pressure. He's going to appoint whom he wants to appoint. In my view, my concern isn't so much whether we have a Latino, another African-American or a woman. That's important. I don't mean to say that it's not, but I want somebody on the court who, although they're conservative, is fair, open-minded, whose vote is in play, who will hear the arguments, who does not come to the court with a mission-driven agenda. That's what the Legal Defense Fund said we wanted with respect to the Roberts nomination. It's what we want with respect to any justice. That's important. I do want to take this moment, though, to say that we also send out our condolences on a personal level to the Rehnquist family. Whatever disappointments we had with getting the chief justice's vote, this is a time for us to recognize that they've suffered a loss and the nation is in mourning, and we join folks in sending condolences.

HOST: Let me--We're running out of time now--just ask a broader question, which is, you two gentlemen, obviously, are legal experts, legal scholars, and legal issues have always been inextricably tied to the advancements of African-Americans in this country. How important is it for ordinary citizens to understand these decisions that the court makes? They're always very complicated and they flash across the front pages. What can people do to better educate themselves about these decisions?

HOST: All right. I'm going to have to stop you there. Unfortunately, GUEST, I don't have another second. I just want to thank you both so much. We are going to obviously keep on this story of the Supreme Court as it evolves. GUEST, president and director-counsel for the NAACP Legal Defense Fund, and Charles Ogletree, law professor at Harvard University. Thank you, gentlemen, for joining us.
GUEST: Thank you.

HOST: You're listening to NEWS & NOTES from NPR News.

[Interview, 2006-04-18, News & Notes]
HOST: Kimberly Samuels and her husband have been organizing bus trips to get displaced voters to the polls in New Orleans. A number of leading Civil Rights groups have teamed to make sure every eligible New Orleans voter who wants to vote can. Their campaign includes a voter's outreach hotline, public service announcements, and voter empowerment centers in cities like Atlanta and Houston.

HOST: We're joined know by GUEST, director counsel and president of the NAACP legal defense fund. He joins us here in our New York Bureau, and at our headquarters in Washington, D.C., Barbara Arwine, executive director of the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under the Law is with us. I thank you both. We greatly appreciate it. Barbara, let me start with you.

HOST: When you hear from a woman like Kimberly Samuels, and you hear all of what she has gone through, talk to us about the bigger picture of the importance of making sure that this election is fair and just.

HOST: All right. Barbara Arnwine, executive director of the Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under the Law, and GUEST, director-counsel and president of the NAACP Legal Defense Fund, I thank you both for joining us.
GUEST: Appreciate it.

HOST: Coming up next, indictments come down in the Duke Lacrosse case; and five black students are arrested in a fraternity hazing incident. We'll discuss these topics and more on our roundtable, up next.

[Interview, 2007-06-28, News & Notes]
HOST: For the other side of the story, I spoke with GUEST, who was leaving the courthouse at the time. He is director-counsel and president of the NAACP Legal Defense and Education Fund. He was also integrally involved in fighting these cases.

HOST: GUEST, thank you so much for coming on. We appreciate it.
GUEST: Thank you.

HOST: GUEST is director-counsel and president of the NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund. We also talked with Democratic presidential candidate John Edwards yesterday before the Supreme Court announced its decision. The former senator from North Carolina admitted he was worried about several recent rulings by the high court.

HOST: Again, that was Democratic presidential candidate John Edwards. To hear our complete interview, tune in tomorrow.

HOST: And one last note before we leave this segment, in California's 37th Congressional District, the death of Congresswoman Juanita Millender-McDonald in April left a power vacuum in the district that includes parts of Compton, South L.A. and Long Beach, but a special election earlier this week has cleared things up a bit.

HOST: African-American Assemblywoman Laura Richardson of Long Beach bested 17 other candidates. The Democrat is heavily favored to win a runoff election is scheduled for August 21st.
